title: Object Pool Pattern
oneLiner: Reuses a pool of expensive, pre-created objects instead of constructing and destroying them on every use.

hero.name: The Recycler
hero.catchphrase: Don't throw it away. Return it, and I'll hand it to the next one who needs it.
hero.power: Keeps a pool of ready-to-use, expensive objects, handing them out and reclaiming them instead of constructing and destroying constantly.
hero.weakness: A borrowed object must be fully reset before it's returned to the pool, or leftover state silently leaks into whoever borrows it next.
hero.origin: The Recycler appeared after a game engine was creating and destroying a new database connection for every single query, tanking throughput under load.

story.problem: Every database query opens a brand-new connection and closes it afterward. Under load, connection setup/teardown dominates response time and the database's max-connections limit gets hit constantly.
story.solution: The Recycler pre-creates a fixed pool of connections at startup. Code borrows a connection, uses it, and returns it — the connection itself is never destroyed between uses.
story.result: Query latency drops sharply since connection setup happens once, not per-request, and the database never sees more than the pool's fixed connection count.

before: A new connection is opened and closed for every query
Connection setup cost is paid on every single request
Easy to exceed the database's max-connections limit
after: A fixed pool of connections is reused across requests
Connection setup cost is paid once, at pool creation
Connection count is capped and predictable

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A metrics dashboard shows connection setup eating 80% of every query's response time.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We're opening and closing a fresh database connection for every single query. No wonder we're hitting connection limits.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Recycler appears holding a rack of ready-to-use connections, each labeled 'available'.
panels.speaker: The Recycler
panels.dialogue: Stop destroying connections after one use. Borrow one from the pool, return it when you're done — I'll keep it ready for the next request.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: pool.acquire() hands out a ready connection. pool.release(conn) resets and returns it to the rack.
panels.speaker: The Recycler
panels.dialogue: The pool is fixed size, created once. Borrowing and returning are cheap — no setup, no teardown, every time.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The dashboard shows query latency dropping by 70%, with connection count now capped and stable.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Latency dropped 70% and we haven't hit a connection limit since. Same database, same queries — just reused connections.

useWhen: Object creation is genuinely expensive (network connections, threads, large buffers) and objects are used repeatedly.
You need to cap the number of concurrent expensive resources in use at once.
Objects can be safely reset to a clean state between uses.
avoidWhen: Object creation is cheap — pooling adds complexity for no measurable benefit.
Objects can't be reliably reset between uses, risking leaked state between borrowers.
Usage is bursty and unpredictable in a way that makes a fixed pool size awkward (either starved or wasteful).
commonMistakes: Forgetting to fully reset an object's state before returning it to the pool, silently leaking data between users.
Sizing the pool incorrectly — too small causes starvation under load, too large wastes resources for no benefit.
Not releasing objects back to the pool on error paths, slowly leaking the pool's capacity over time.
Confusing Object Pool with Flyweight — Pool reuses whole objects exclusively one-at-a-time; Flyweight shares immutable state across many objects simultaneously.
explanation.realWorldExample: Database connection pools, thread pools, and game engines pooling bullets/particles/enemies that are frequently spawned and destroyed are all Object Pool in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from Flyweight? Both are about reuse.

conversation.speaker: The Recycler
conversation.message: Flyweight shares one immutable piece of data across many objects AT THE SAME TIME. I hand out whole, exclusive objects ONE AT A TIME — you borrow it, use it, give it back before anyone else can.

conversation.speaker: The Recycler
conversation.message: Leftover state. If you don't reset an object before returning it, the next borrower inherits your mess — and that bug is brutal to trace back to the pool.

codeBattle.scenario: Your PDF-generation service creates a new heavyweight rendering engine instance for every request, and engine startup alone takes 300ms under a load of hundreds of requests per second.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Recycler keeps a fixed pool of already-started rendering engines ready to borrow, eliminating the 300ms startup cost from the request path entirely.

quiz.question: What problem does Object Pool solve?
options: Repeatedly creating and destroying expensive objects wastes time and resources
Two incompatible interfaces need to work together
An object needs to notify many listeners of a change
A class needs to guarantee exactly one instance
quiz.answer: Repeatedly creating and destroying expensive objects wastes time and resources
quiz.explanation: Object Pool's entire value is amortizing expensive construction cost across many reuses instead of paying it every time.

quiz.question: What must happen before a pooled object is handed to a new borrower?
options: It must be reset to a clean state, or leftover data leaks between users
It must be destroyed and rebuilt from scratch
It must be cloned into a new instance
Nothing — pooled objects don't need any preparation
quiz.answer: It must be reset to a clean state, or leftover data leaks between users
quiz.explanation: Skipping the reset step is the single most common and dangerous Object Pool bug.

quiz.question: How does Object Pool differ from Flyweight?
options: Object Pool hands out whole objects exclusively, one at a time; Flyweight shares immutable state across many objects simultaneously
They are the exact same pattern with different names
Flyweight requires a database; Object Pool does not
Object Pool can only be used with database connections
quiz.answer: Object Pool hands out whole objects exclusively, one at a time; Flyweight shares immutable state across many objects simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Pool grants exclusive, temporary ownership; Flyweight grants concurrent, shared access to immutable data.

quiz.question: When is Object Pool the wrong choice?
options: When object creation is already cheap, making pooling unnecessary complexity
When object creation involves a network connection or thread setup
When you need to cap the number of concurrent expensive resources
When objects can be safely reset between uses
quiz.answer: When object creation is already cheap, making pooling unnecessary complexity
quiz.explanation: Pooling only pays off when construction cost is real — for cheap objects, it's pure overhead.
